summary:
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands and stand under the national framework: the Dutch civil-status and anti-discrimination law in force in the European Netherlands applies here in the same form, with no separate island legislation on marriage or discrimination operating alongside it.

No source in the inventory describes a provision that addresses trans visitors directly. The protection that exists on these islands is carried by marriage registration and general anti-discrimination law, not by text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities.

The Census Office in Saba registered the Caribbean Netherlands' first same-sex union on 4 December 2012: Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez (26) wed Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto (27), both visiting residents. Same-sex unions have therefore been registrable in these islands since 2012, and the island registry has performed one for visitors. This 2012 registration is the only dated union event in the sources; no later instance is documented.

For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex, that registration evidences a working route rather than a paper right. Civil ceremonies on Saba run through the island registry, with the Court Room in the Administrative Building recorded as the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony and registrar Julieta Woods documented as flexible about couples' wishes. Full destination-wedding suppliers, including caterers, florists and accommodation, operate on the island.
tangentialFactors:
GayCities (published 14 December 2022, updated 1 September 2023) places Bonaire at #5 in a "Top 10 destinations that celebrate marriage equality in the Caribbean and Latin America" list, stating that as a territory of the Netherlands its citizens and visitors are protected by strict anti-discrimination laws and that same-sex couples are warmly welcomed. This is a publication's editorial ranking of destinations, not a measurement of risk, enforcement or trans-specific conditions, and it makes no finding about gender identity, markers or facilities.

The inventory contains no comparative figure for these islands against other Caribbean jurisdictions on trans-specific violence, screening practice or legal recognition, so no ranking of the islands' relative safety can be drawn from it.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are covered by the Dutch anti-discrimination law as applied in the islands, with no island equality statute of their own operating beside it. Protection therefore runs through the general statute rather than through any provision naming gender identity.

The island registry on Saba performs civil ceremonies as a routine public function, documented through its official tourism service, and it registered a union for two visiting residents on 4 December 2012. Residents seeking recognition of a relationship classed locally as same-sex use the same registry route.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses airport or seaport screening, document or marker rules, gendered facilities, healthcare access, hate-crime enforcement or violence data for these islands. Whether the anti-discrimination law has been invoked on gender-identity grounds here, and how it has been enforced, is not sourced.

The 4 December 2012 union is the only dated registration event in the sources; no later instance is documented, and the absence of later records is not evidence either way about current practice.

The GayCities ranking is editorial framing by a travel publication and is not a risk assessment; it is carried here as evidence of how the island presents itself, not as a finding about conditions on the ground.
